content: The scapula, commonly referred to as the shoulder blade, is a flat, triangular bone that connects the humerus (arm bone) to the clavicle (collarbone). It forms the posterior portion of the shoulder girdle. In humans, the scapula has two surfaces, three borders, and three angles. On the anterior (front) surface of the scapula lies the subscapular fossa, a concave area where the subscapularis muscle attaches. The posterior surface is divided by a prominent bony ridge called the spine of the scapula into two regions: the supraspinous fossa above and the infraspinous fossa below. The spine of the scapula begins flat at the base of the shoulder bone, ascends to a peak known as the tuber scapulae, and then sharply declines in height. In humans, carnivores, and bovines, the spine extends into a forward-projecting hook called the acromion, which continues beyond the main body of the bone. Another hook-like projection, the coracoid process, arises from the lateral angle of the scapula. The tip of the coracoid process serves as an attachment site for several muscles, including the coracobrachialis. Near the base of the coracoid process, also at the lateral angle, is a depression called the glenoid cavity. This cavity forms the socket for the head of the humerus, creating the glenohumeral joint. Additionally, the scapula articulates with the clavicle at the acromion process, forming the acromioclavicular joint. The scapula's surfaces are specialized for muscle attachment. The costal (ventral) surface features the subscapular fossa, which is marked by oblique ridges in its medial two-thirds. These ridges provide attachment points for the tendinous insertions of the subscapularis muscle, while the smooth lateral third is covered by the muscle's fibers. The subscapular fossa is separated from the vertebral border by smooth triangular areas at the medial and inferior angles, which, along with a narrow ridge between them, provide attachment for the serratus anterior muscle. A transverse depression at the upper part of the fossa, known as the subscapular angle, strengthens the bone's structure by forming an arched shape that supports the spine and acromion. The dorsal surface of the scapula is arched and divided into two unequal parts by the spine. The smaller supraspinous fossa, located above the spine, is concave, smooth, and broader medially. It provides the origin for the supraspinatus muscle. The larger infraspinous fossa, below the spine, features a shallow concavity near its vertebral margin, a prominent convexity at its center, and a deep groove near the axillary border. The medial two-thirds of the infraspinous fossa give origin to the infraspinatus muscle, while the lateral third is covered by this muscle. A ridge near the inferior angle serves as an attachment for a fibrous septum that separates the infraspinatus from the teres major and teres minor muscles. The lower third of the infraspinous fossa provides origin for the teres major muscle and serves as a gliding surface for the latissimus dorsi, which may also originate from this area. The acromion, a large, flat, triangular or oblong process, forms the summit of the shoulder. It projects laterally, then curves forward and upward to overhang the glenoid cavity. The scapula has three borders: the superior border, which is the shortest and thinnest; the axillary (lateral) border, which is the thickest and extends obliquely downward from the glenoid cavity to the inferior angle; and the vertebral (medial) border, which is the longest and runs from the medial to the inferior angle. The three angles of the scapula are the medial (superior) angle, the inferior angle, and the lateral angle. Structurally, the head, processes, and thickened parts of the scapula contain cancellous (spongy) bone, while the rest consists of a thin layer of compact bone. The central part of the supraspinous fossa and the upper part of the infraspinous fossa are often so thin that they may appear semitransparent. In some cases, the bone may be absent in these areas, leaving only fibrous tissue separating the adjacent muscles.
